title: The Odyssey
subtitle: The Long Way Home
attribution: An original abridged adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey
intro: The same ship. A crew still trying to reach Ithaca.
ending: His friends were themselves again. The journey was not over.
description: Odysseus and his remaining companions follow a gift of wind, lose their way, and land on Circe’s island.
stageLabel: Odysseus remembers the journey toward Ithaca

adaptationSource.title: Homer, Odyssey, Book X
adaptationSource.note: Original abridged English dialogue and narration. Eurylochus and Polites represent the surviving crew. Two ships represent the lost fleet. Circe receives the scouts in her courtyard for visible staging. Her domestic episode is condensed to transformation and release; the year on Aeaea and departure continue in Chapter 6. No graphic violence.

steps.text: Odysseus and Eurylochus were back aboard their ship. Behind them lay the cave they had escaped.
Polites had stayed with the ship while they entered the cave. Now he kept watch beside them. He, too, wanted to reach Ithaca.
Two other ships were waiting farther out. They carried more of the men who had sailed from Troy with Odysseus. Their crews had stayed at sea.
The ships sailed on together. After more days at sea, they reached the island of Aeolus, the keeper of the winds.
A stone path led up from the landing to Aeolus’s court. Odysseus would speak with him. Eurylochus and Polites would wait with the ship.
Aeolus welcomed Odysseus into his court. Odysseus told him about Troy and the long journey home.
“You have carried the war a long way.”
“I would rather carry it home.”
Aeolus held out a leather bag. Its neck was tied shut with a silver cord.
“I have put the winds that would drive you away from home inside this bag. Keep it closed.”
Odysseus took the bag. Aeolus left one gentle wind free to carry all three ships toward Ithaca.
“Leave the knot alone until you are home,” Aeolus warned.
Odysseus returned to the same ship with the bag in his hand. He told Eurylochus and Polites to keep it closed.
The island fell behind them. The gentle wind filled their sails and carried the ships toward home.
For nine days, all three ships followed the gentle wind. Odysseus stayed awake to steer. The closed bag lay beside him.
“Let someone else steer for a while,” Eurylochus said.
“When we reach the shore,” Odysseus answered.

transition.reason: On the tenth morning the same ships approach Ithaca

steps.text: On the tenth morning, Ithaca lay ahead. Odysseus could see its rocky shore, green trees and houses.
“There. We are almost home.”
Eurylochus and Polites looked toward the land with him. After so much traveling, their homes were close.
At last, Odysseus could stay awake no longer. He fell asleep on deck beside the bag.
Polites looked at the silver cord. He began to wonder what Aeolus had put inside the bag.
“Could it be gold?” Polites asked. “Why does he keep it closed?”
“Aeolus said it would help us reach home,” Eurylochus answered.
Polites untied the cord. There was no gold inside. The trapped winds rushed out of the open bag.
The wind pulled the ships away from Ithaca. Odysseus woke as the shore disappeared behind them.
“We could see it.”
Polites had no answer. The bag was empty, and the ships were moving away from home.
The winds drove all three ships back to Aeolus’s island. Odysseus brought his ship toward the same landing.
Odysseus showed Aeolus the empty bag. He explained what had happened and asked for help again.
“I will not give you the winds a second time,” Aeolus said. “You must leave my island.”
Odysseus returned without another gift. He told his companions they would have to row.
Eurylochus and Polites took their places beside Odysseus. The crews of the other ships rowed with them.
For six days, the men rowed. Odysseus, Eurylochus and Polites stayed aboard the same ship. The other two ships followed.
They found a harbor surrounded by high cliffs. The other crews entered it. Odysseus kept his ship outside the narrow opening, where he could turn back.
The people of this shore were giants. Two stood on the ground above the cliff, each holding a great stone over his head.
Both giants threw at once. Each stone struck a ship, breaking both hulls. Those crews were killed. Only Odysseus’s ship, outside the opening, could escape.
“Row. Now.”
Odysseus’s ship moved away from the opening. Eurylochus and Polites were still beside him. Behind them lay the wrecks of the other ships.
Their ship was the only one left. After more time at sea, they reached Aeaea, an island covered with trees.
They brought the ship to the shore and rested. When they were ready, Odysseus asked Eurylochus and Polites to look inland for food.
Odysseus stayed aboard to guard the ship. Eurylochus and Polites would follow the sandy path through the trees.
The path led to a stone house. Eurylochus and Polites stopped in its clearing. The door stood open.
“Someone lives here. Let us ask for food.”
Polites approached the doorway to ask for food. Eurylochus waited farther down the path, outside the house.
Circe, the woman who lived in the house, came out to welcome Polites. She carried a cup and led him toward her table.
Eurylochus remained on the path. Polites accepted Circe’s welcome and waited for the drink.
Polites drank from the cup. Circe took it back and raised her wand toward him.
Polites became a pig. He could still think like a person, but he could no longer speak to his companion.
From the path, Eurylochus saw what had happened to Polites. He turned back toward the shore to warn Odysseus.
“Circe turned Polites into a pig,” Eurylochus said. “Do not go there. We have lost enough.”
“Stay with the ship,” Odysseus told Eurylochus. “I will go and bring Polites back.”
On the path to Circe’s house, Odysseus met Hermes. The messenger carried a white flower with a black root.
“This plant is called moly,” Hermes said. “Keep it with you. It will stop Circe’s drink from changing your shape.”
Odysseus took the plant. Now he could reach Polites without being changed into an animal himself.
He reached the same clearing. Circe stood beside her table, and Polites was still a pig nearby.
Odysseus drank while keeping the moly in his other hand. The plant protected him. He stayed a man.
“Promise that you will not hurt us,” Odysseus said. “Give Polites his own body back.”
Circe promised to stop harming them. She turned her wand toward Polites.
Polites was himself again. Odysseus sent him down the path to tell Eurylochus that it was safe to come to the house.
At the landing, Eurylochus saw Polites walking toward him as a man again. Polites told him that Odysseus was waiting at the house.
The ship stayed at the landing while Eurylochus followed Polites back up the path. It would wait for their next journey.
Eurylochus reached the clearing with Polites. All three companions were together again, and Circe had promised to leave them unharmed.
“Rest here,” Circe said. “I will give you food and a safe place to sleep.”
This time, they chose to stay and recover their strength. Their ship waited at the shore. When they were ready, the journey to Ithaca would continue.
